description: Published numerical results transcribed for visual exploration. These are aggregate statistics, not respondent records. See survey-derived.json for independently recomputed results from the public survey archive.

typology.title: A typology of US parents' mental loads: Core and episodic cognitive labor
typology.note: Online-first PDF is dated 2024; journal issue is 2025, 87(3), 966-989.
typology.sample: Individual US parents, including single parents and same-sex partnerships; not matched couples.
typology.rounding: Task response percentages are rounded to whole numbers. Response totals may be 99 or 101; do not silently normalise them.

followup.title: Take a Load Off? Not for Mothers: Gender, Cognitive Labor, and the Limits of Time and Money
followup.sample: Partnered heterosexual US parents, restricted from the same 2023 survey. Not an independent replication or longitudinal follow-up.
followup.model_source: Table 2, first three predictor rows; Table 3, first three predictor rows
followup.model: Gender-specific negative binomial regressions; adjusted associations, not causal effects.
followup.high_income_definition: Personal annual salary including bonuses and commissions of at least US$100,000; not household income or pounds sterling.
followup.care_definition: Self-reported hours per week looking after family members, including children, elderly, ill or disabled family members; broader than childcare alone.
followup.housework_definition: Self-reported hours per week on household work such as cooking, cleaning and yard work, excluding childcare and leisure.

survey_archive.title: Replication Data for: The Political Consequences of the Mental Load
survey_archive.author: Weeks, Ana
survey_archive.note: Archive formally accompanies a third paper using the same survey. Validate variables and results against the two target papers; do not label this a replication package published for either target paper.

response_unit: Percent of the specified respondent gender selecting each response. Other combines someone else and not applicable in published Table 2.

typology_summary.note: Both the single-item and task-based measures are self-reports. Their difference is a measurement mismatch, not objective proof of exaggeration. The item-based proportions account for applicable tasks; they are not the simple average of the Table 2 percentages.

notes: P values print as .00; this is rounding, not a zero probability. Exact p values are not supplied here.
The published 66.96 percent does not equal (13.72-8.18)/8.18*100, which is about 67.73 percent. Preserve the published value for audit; prefer the raw task counts in graphics.
Some published differences differ from subtraction of rounded means, e.g. scheduling 1.60 versus 1.61. Preserve both source precision and provenance.

followup_models.se_definition: Published transformed standard error, computed by the delta method.

comparison_definitions.employed: Paid employment versus not in paid employment
comparison_definitions.high_income: Personal salary >= US$100,000 versus lower salary
comparison_definitions.earns_more: Higher income than partner versus not higher

rows.note: Publisher HTML shows three stars; indexed PDF shows two. Both indicate p < .01. Do not resolve this discrepancy by invention.

notes: Convert to relative percent difference with 100*(irr-1), not a percentage-point difference.
An insignificant estimate is not evidence of an exactly zero effect. Retain the 0.95 and 1.03 estimates rather than snapping them to 1.
Do not combine these separate comparisons into a salary slider or a simulated career progression. They are cross-sectional associations.

Reported standard errors and significance stars do not always agree under a naive Wald calculation. Preserve the published values; do not manufacture publication-quality confidence intervals from rounded entries.
